When Wes married Rachel, he was a well-established photographer who supported her through cooking school. Ten years later, the digital revolution had hit his business hard. His wife, Rachel, had just become head chef at a respected restaurant. She was thrilled and afraid she would not measure up. Each time she confided that fear, Wes brushed it aside and told her to be more positive. He thought he was supporting her. Rachel heard condescension, and said nothing about how much it hurt. Wes was full of doubt himself. Had anyone asked them then, both would have ruled out an affair.

Jinashree Rajendrakumar lays out a pattern like this in How Do Affairs Happen?. She calls it the Gottman-Rusbult-Glass Cascade. It has eight steps that play out over time. Here we follow only the overall trajectory, and her article covers every step in full. The cascade starts when emotional bids are “met with turning away or against instead of turning toward.” In her words, repeated failed bids make trust erode “gradually.”

blocks.x: A bid for emotional connection is a gesture, a question or a confidence that asks a partner for attention or support. In Gottman terms, each time Rachel confided her fear, she was making a bid. Each time Wes answered with cheerful advice, he was turning away.

Further down the cascade comes the negative comparison, which Brandon Leuangpaseuth, who writes about his own affair in What to Do After an Affair, defines as “a harmful comparison of one’s partner to someone else.”
Too Close to Someone Else
https://www.gottman.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/LoveNotesLeadMagnet-WebsiteThumbnailCover_EmotionalLiteracy_1080x1350_v1.webp

The weeks went by. The table became theirs. Wes began shaving with extra care on the days he hoped to see Tess, without admitting why even to himself. Tess told him online dating had not worked out. “I can’t believe someone as great as you can’t get a date,” Wes said. Then he caught himself.

When a Chaplin festival came to the local cinema, asking Tess seemed only natural. Rachel was busy at the restaurant and hated silent films anyway. Soon they were going to the movies, always on nights when Rachel worked late. Wes never mentioned Tess to Rachel. She might misunderstand, he thought. He called it a small secret. Tess knew he was married, and he told himself he was doing nothing wrong.
https://www.gottman.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/New-Gottman-Relationship-Adviser_Product-Image-062122_1080x1080_v1.png
blocks.c: Gottman Relationship Adviser Product Image, two faces touching at the noses

Walls and Windows

Wes began to confide in Tess about his marriage. He also told her something Rachel did not know: he was hoping for a good position at an advertising agency. When the job went to another candidate, he was so crushed that Rachel could see something was wrong. “If you had told me about it,” she said, “maybe I could have helped you prepare for the interviews. Even if you don’t think so, I know a thing or two myself.”
https://www.gottman.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/AAL-HTMYRW-1000-x-1000-px-1.png
blocks.c: Gottman Relationship Coach How to Make Your Relationship Work

blocks.x: Wes said, “I don’t need your help.”

The next day Tess hugged him and praised his photographs without reservation. She made him feel believed in. Rachel, he told himself, did not. In his eyes, Tess was now prettier and sexier than Rachel. She was also much kinder to him.

Dr. Shirley Glass spent more than two decades studying infidelity. In her book Not “Just Friends”, she uses walls and windows as an analogy for a healthy marriage: a wall keeps outsiders from invading the couple’s heart, and a window keeps the partners open to each other. Rajendrakumar describes the result: “The window between the partners is replaced with a wall, as the window opens up to outsiders.” She adds: “Secrets begin with omission.” Wes had kept Tess from Rachel. Now he had kept the interviews from her too.
https://www.gottman.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/October-2026-Virtual-ASL_Laura-and-Zach_1080x1350_v1-1.jpg
What People Seek in an Affair

Eventually Wes and Tess became lovers. On the question of whether affairs are the root cause of divorce, Dr. John Gottman writes in The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work: “In most cases, it’s the other way around. Problems in the marriage that send the couple on a trajectory to divorce also send one (or both) of them looking for intimate connection outside the marriage.” He adds that secret meetings between lovers, which he calls trysts, “are usually not about sex but about seeking friendship, support, understanding, respect, attention, caring, and concern.”
